summary: Turns a folder into God Mode (All Tasks): about 200 Control Panel settings and admin tools in one searchable window.
example: Right-click the desktop > New > Folder, rename it to this exact text, press Enter; the icon turns into Control Panel

summary: Opens the same God Mode window straight from the Run box, without creating a folder.
Opens Windows Tools (formerly Administrative Tools): Event Viewer, Services, Disk Cleanup, Task Scheduler and more in one folder.
Opens Network Connections, where you can disable, re-enable or set custom DNS on Wi-Fi and Ethernet adapters.
Opens Credential Manager to review or remove saved Windows, network-share and app sign-ins.
Opens classic Power Options to switch power plans and choose what the power button and laptop lid do.
Opens classic Programs and Features, the fast uninstall list that also shows install dates and sizes.
Opens All Control Panel Items as one icon list, skipping the category view.
Opens your Startup folder; any shortcut placed here launches automatically when you sign in.
example: Win+R, type shell:startup, Enter, then drop an app shortcut in

summary: Opens the Send to folder so you can add your own folders and apps to the right-click Send to menu.
Shows every installed app, Store apps included; drag any of them onto the desktop to make a shortcut.
Opens your Roaming AppData folder, where many apps keep their settings, plugins and some game saves.
Opens Pictures\Screenshots, where Win+PrtScn saves full-screen captures.
Opens System Information: exact CPU, motherboard, BIOS version and date, installed RAM and whether Secure Boot is on.
Opens the DirectX Diagnostic Tool: GPU model, video memory, driver version and display details, with a Save All Information button.
Opens Device Manager to update, roll back or reinstall drivers; yellow warning icons flag problem devices.
Opens Disk Management to see every drive and partition, change drive letters and set up a new disk.
Opens Resource Monitor, showing which programs use CPU, memory, disk and network right now in more detail than Task Manager.
Opens Reliability Monitor, a day-by-day timeline of app crashes, failed updates and hardware errors.
Opens Windows Memory Diagnostic, which restarts the PC and tests your RAM for faults.
Opens Disk Cleanup; click "Clean up system files" to also remove leftover Windows Update files.
Opens System Properties to rename the PC, turn on System Restore, trim visual effects and edit environment variables.
Lists each drive's model and health status (OK, Pred Fail); WMIC was removed from Windows 11 24H2+ in August 2026, so use Get-PhysicalDisk there.
install: Built in on Windows 10 only (removed from Windows 11 24H2 and later)

summary: Read-only check of drive C:'s file system that reports errors without fixing them; run Command Prompt as admin.
Fixes file-system errors on the drive; because C: is in use, it offers to run at the next restart.
Does everything /f does, plus scans every sector for bad spots and recovers readable data; can take hours on a large hard drive.
Scans the drive online without locking it, so you can keep working while it checks for file-system errors.
Repairs the Windows component store using Windows Update; run it before sfc /scannow from an admin prompt.
Scans protected Windows system files and replaces corrupted ones; run it after DISM, as admin.
Clears superseded update files out of the Windows component store to free disk space; run as admin.
Lists Windows edition and build, install date, last boot time, RAM, BIOS version and installed updates.
Shows whether each drive is BitLocker-encrypted and how far encryption has progressed; run as admin.
Searches the Windows Package Manager catalog and shows each app's exact ID.
Installs an app by its exact ID, with no website or installer hunting.
Updates every app winget can see; run plain winget upgrade first to preview the list.
Saves a list of your installed apps; on a new PC, winget import -i apps.json reinstalls them all.
Saves an HTML battery report: design vs. current full-charge capacity, cycle count and usage history.
Builds an HTML report of recent Modern Standby sleep sessions, showing what drained the battery while the lid was shut.
Watches the PC for 60 seconds, then writes energy-report.html listing power and battery-life problems; run as admin.
Lists apps and drivers currently keeping the screen on or blocking sleep; run as admin.
Shows what woke the PC from its last sleep, such as a mouse, network adapter or wake timer.
Shows every adapter's IP address, MAC address, gateway, DNS servers and DHCP lease.
Clears the DNS cache, often fixing sites that won't load after a DNS or hosting change.
Pings nonstop until Ctrl+C, handy for spotting Wi-Fi dropouts; plain ping sends four and stops.
Lists every hop between your PC and a site, showing where a connection slows down or breaks.
Looks up a domain's IP address; add a DNS server's address to compare its answer.
Lists all connections and listening ports with the process ID behind each, which you can match in Task Manager.

command: netsh wlan show profile name="WiFiName" key=clear
summary: Reveals a saved Wi-Fi network's password under Key Content; netsh wlan show profiles lists saved names. Run as admin.
example: netsh wlan show profile name="HomeWiFi" key=clear

summary: Builds an HTML report of the last three days of Wi-Fi sessions and disconnects; run as admin.
example: netsh wlan show wlanreport, then open C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\WlanReport\wlan-report-latest.html

summary: Lists running processes with their process IDs and memory use.
Force-closes a frozen program by its process name.
Restarts straight into Advanced Startup for Safe Mode, System Restore or booting from a USB drive.
Installs Windows Subsystem for Linux with Ubuntu by default (-d picks another distro); run as admin and restart when asked.
Lists installed Linux distros, whether each is running and which WSL version it uses.
Copies a folder and all its subfolders, skipping files that haven't changed; ideal for repeat backups to an external drive.
The modern replacement for wmic diskdrive: lists each drive with its health (Healthy, Warning, Unhealthy) and operational status.
example: Get-PhysicalDisk | Select FriendlyName, MediaType, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus

summary: Shows SMART-style counters for each drive: temperature, wear, read/write errors and power-on hours; run PowerShell as admin.
example: Get-PhysicalDisk | Get-StorageReliabilityCounter | Select-Object DeviceId, Temperature, Wear, ReadErrorsTotal, WriteErrorsTotal, PowerOnHours

summary: Runs TRIM on an SSD or defragments a hard drive, the same job as Defragment and Optimize Drives; run as admin.
Dumps detailed Windows, BIOS and hardware info; pick the fields you want with Select-Object.
example: Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object OsName, OsVersion, CsModel, BiosSMBIOSBIOSVersion

summary: Shows the PC's serial number for warranty lookups, replacing the removed wmic bios get serialnumber.
Lists the ten processes that have used the most CPU time since they started.
Restarts the Print Spooler, the quick fix for a stuck print queue; run as admin.
Lists connected devices with driver or hardware problems, the same ones Device Manager flags.
Checks whether a server and a specific port are reachable, with ping and route details.
Looks up DNS records for a domain; -Server chooses which DNS server to ask.
Prints a file's SHA-256 hash to match against the checksum on the download page.

command: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 FullName, Length
summary: Finds the ten largest files under the current folder, Windows' answer to du for tracking down space hogs.
example: cd $HOME; Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 FullName, Length

summary: Downloads a file from a URL, PowerShell's built-in answer to wget.
Shows Microsoft Defender's status: whether real-time protection is on, when it last scanned and how fresh its virus definitions are.
Runs a Microsoft Defender quick scan from the command line; use FullScan to check every file.
Creates a System Restore point before a risky change; needs admin and System Protection on, allows one per 24 hours, Windows PowerShell 5.1 only.
Shows the 20 most recent errors in the System event log without opening Event Viewer.
Keeps the display and Mac awake until you press Ctrl+C; -t sets a time limit in seconds.
Stops the Mac idle-sleeping only while a long command runs, then lets it sleep normally.
Shows battery percentage, whether it's charging and the estimated time remaining.
Lists what is currently preventing sleep, such as a video call, download or app.
Turns Low Power Mode on for both battery and charger; 0 turns it back off.
Apple's built-in speed test: download and upload speed plus responsiveness under load, no website needed.
Prints your Mac's local IP address on Wi-Fi, which is en0 on most Macs.
Flushes the DNS cache when websites fail to load after a DNS or network change.
Runs a Spotlight search from Terminal across file names and contents; -onlyin limits it to one folder.
Finds files by name only, instantly, using the Spotlight index.
Copies a command's output straight to the clipboard; pbpaste pastes it back out.
Converts an image to another format, here iPhone HEIC to JPG, with the Mac's built-in image tool.
Prints a download's SHA-256 checksum to compare with the one the publisher lists.
Saves screenshots to a folder of your choice instead of cluttering the Desktop; create the folder first.
example: mkdir -p ~/Pictures/Screenshots && defaults write com.apple.screencapture location ~/Pictures/Screenshots && killall SystemUIServer

summary: Switches the screenshot format from PNG to smaller JPG files; heic, pdf and tiff also work.
example: defaults write com.apple.screencapture type jpg && killall SystemUIServer

summary: Removes the large drop shadow from window screenshots.
example: defaults write com.apple.screencapture disable-shadow -bool true && killall SystemUIServer

summary: Always shows hidden files in Finder; Cmd+Shift+. toggles them temporarily instead.
example: defaults write com.apple.finder AppleShowAllFiles -bool true && killall Finder

summary: Adds a path bar to the bottom of Finder windows showing exactly which folder you're in.
example: defaults write com.apple.finder ShowPathbar -bool true && killall Finder

summary: Shows every file extension in Finder, so a file like invoice.pdf.app can't pass itself off as a PDF.
example: defaults write NSGlobalDomain AppleShowAllExtensions -bool true && killall Finder

summary: Makes an auto-hiding Dock appear instantly instead of after a short pause.
example: defaults write com.apple.dock autohide-delay -float 0 && killall Dock

summary: Undoes any defaults tweak by removing it, which restores the macOS default.
example: defaults delete com.apple.dock autohide-delay && killall Dock

summary: Shows the macOS version and build number.
Shows your Mac's model, chip, memory, serial number and firmware version.
Lists available macOS updates; sudo softwareupdate -i -a installs all of them.
Shows details on the internal drive, including its SMART status (Verified means healthy).
Starts a Time Machine backup right now; tmutil latestbackup shows where the last one is saved.
Installs command-line tools and apps from Homebrew, the Mac's most popular package manager; brew upgrade updates them all.
Prints a full system report (CPU, GPU, RAM, kernel, drivers, disks, network) with serial numbers and IPs masked, so it's safe to share.
install: sudo apt install inxi (Fedora: sudo dnf install inxi · Arch: sudo pacman -S inxi)

summary: Shows distro, kernel, desktop, CPU, GPU, RAM and uptime beside your distro's logo; the maintained successor to the archived neofetch.
install: sudo apt install fastfetch (Debian 13+, Ubuntu 26.04+ · Fedora: sudo dnf install fastfetch · Arch: sudo pacman -S fastfetch)

summary: Shows the kernel version, hostname and CPU architecture; uname -r prints just the kernel version.
Shows your distro's name and version, e.g. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, or Debian 13 (trixie) on current Raspberry Pi OS.
Shows total, used and available RAM and swap in GB or MB; "available" is what apps can still use.
Lists connected USB devices, a quick check that a webcam, adapter or dev board has been detected.
install: Built in on most distros (else sudo apt install usbutils)

summary: Shows CPU, GPU and motherboard temperatures plus fan speeds, useful for gaming and tracking down overheating.
install: sudo apt install lm-sensors && sudo sensors-detect (Fedora: sudo dnf install lm_sensors · Arch: sudo pacman -S lm_sensors)

summary: Lists every file, hidden dotfiles included, with sizes in K/M/G, permissions, owner and last-modified date.
Draws a folder's structure as a tree, here limited to two levels deep.
Sends files to the desktop Trash instead of deleting them permanently, so a mistake can be undone.
Searches the current folder and everything below it for a file by name; -iname ignores case and * works as a wildcard.
Lists every file over 500 MB below the current folder, a fast way to find space hogs.
Searches inside every file in a folder for text, ignoring case and showing file names with line numbers.
Finds files by name across the whole system instantly, using a prebuilt index.
install: sudo apt install plocate (sudo updatedb refreshes the index)

summary: Shows the size of each folder in your home directory, sorted so the biggest land at the bottom.
Interactive disk-usage browser: folders are sorted biggest first and arrow keys drill down, so storage hogs stand out fast.
install: sudo apt install ncdu (Fedora: sudo dnf install ncdu · Arch: sudo pacman -S ncdu)

summary: Shows size, used and free space for every mounted drive and partition.
Lists drives and partitions with filesystem type, label, free space and mount point.
Reads a drive's SMART health data: overall PASSED/FAILED, reallocated sectors, power-on hours and temperature.
Live, colorful task manager for CPU, RAM and every process; F6 sorts, F3 searches and F9 closes a program.
install: sudo apt install htop (Fedora: sudo dnf install htop · Arch: sudo pacman -S htop)

summary: Modern resource monitor with live graphs for CPU, memory, disks, network and processes.
Closes every process matching a name with no PID lookup needed; kill PID targets a single process.
Reruns a command every second in full screen, handy for watching temperatures, downloads or free space.
Lists each network interface with its state and IP address, one line per interface.
Prints this machine's local IP addresses, handy for SSHing in from another device.
Lists listening ports and, with sudo, the program behind each one; the modern replacement for netstat.
Sends four pings then stops, showing whether a host is reachable and how long replies take.
Lists each network hop between you and a server, showing where a connection slows down or dies.
Combines traceroute and ping into a live view of packet loss at every hop, ideal for finding the bad link.
Looks up a domain's IP address; add @1.1.1.1 to ask a specific DNS server and compare answers.
install: sudo apt install bind9-dnsutils (Fedora: bind-utils · Arch: bind)

summary: Downloads a file from a link straight into the current folder, no browser needed; -c resumes an interrupted download.
install: Built in on most distros (else sudo apt install wget)

summary: Lists nearby Wi-Fi networks with signal strength, channel and security type.
install: Built in on NetworkManager distros (Ubuntu, Fedora, Raspberry Pi OS)

summary: Text menus for joining Wi-Fi, editing connections or setting a static IP without learning nmcli syntax.
install: Built in on NetworkManager distros (Ubuntu, Fedora, Raspberry Pi OS)

command: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
summary: Refreshes the package list, then installs every available update on Debian, Ubuntu, Mint and Pop!_OS.
example: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

summary: Installs a program and everything it needs from your distro's repositories; apt search keyword finds package names.
Removes leftover packages that nothing installed needs anymore, freeing disk space.
Refreshes repositories and installs all updates on Fedora (dnf5 since Fedora 41).
Installs a package and its dependencies on Fedora and other Red Hat-family distros; dnf search keyword finds names.
Syncs repositories and upgrades the whole system on Arch, Manjaro and EndeavourOS.
Installs a package on Arch-based distros; pacman -Ss keyword searches the repositories.
Installs a sandboxed app from Flathub that runs the same on any distro.
install: sudo apt install flatpak, then flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo (preinstalled on Fedora and Mint)

summary: Updates every installed Flatpak app and runtime in one go.
install: sudo apt install flatpak (preinstalled on Fedora and Mint)

summary: Removes runtimes that no installed app uses anymore, often freeing gigabytes.
install: sudo apt install flatpak (preinstalled on Fedora and Mint)

summary: Shows whether a service is running, since when, and its most recent log lines.
Restarts a service after a config change or when it hangs.
Starts a service right away and sets it to start on every boot.
Lists services that failed to start, the first place to look when something breaks after boot.
Ranks services by how long they took during boot, so you can see what slows startup.
Shows only error messages from the current boot; -b -1 shows the previous boot, useful after a crash.
Follows one service's log live as new lines arrive.
Deletes system logs older than two weeks to reclaim space; check their size first with journalctl --disk-usage.
Makes a script or downloaded program executable so you can run it.
Sets permissions by number: 644 means you edit and others read, 755 adds run rights, 600 keeps it private to you.
Changes who owns a file or folder, fixing "permission denied" on files that were created with sudo.
Adds you to a group, e.g. docker to run Docker without sudo or dialout for serial boards; log out and back in afterward.
Packs a folder into one compressed .tar.gz file.
Extracts a .tar.gz archive; add -C folder to extract it somewhere else.
Creates a .zip archive that opens natively on Windows and macOS.
Extracts a .zip into the folder you choose.
Copies your SSH public key to another machine so future logins need no password.
install: Built in with the OpenSSH client

summary: Copies or syncs folders, transferring only new and changed files with a progress readout; ideal for backups.
install: Built in on most distros (else sudo apt install rsync)

summary: Syncs a folder to another machine over SSH with compression; rerunning it only sends what's missing or changed.
install: Built in on most distros (else sudo apt install rsync)

summary: Searches your command history for anything matching a keyword; rerun a result with !number.
Searches your history as you type; press Ctrl+R again for older matches and Enter to run the one shown.
Reruns your previous command with sudo, for when it failed with "permission denied".
Shows short, practical examples for a command instead of the full manual page.
install: sudo apt install tealdeer, then tldr --update (Fedora/Arch: tealdeer)

summary: Prints a file's SHA-256 checksum so you can match it against the one on the download page.
Keeps terminal sessions running after you disconnect; detach with Ctrl+B then D, and return with tmux attach.
Shows the Pi's processor temperature; the CPU starts throttling between 80 and 85°C.
Flags power and heat trouble: throttled=0x0 is healthy, while 0x50000 means under-voltage and throttling happened since boot, so check the power supply.
Shows the current CPU clock speed in Hz, a quick check of whether the Pi is running at full speed.
Text menu for enabling SSH, VNC, I2C, SPI and serial, and setting hostname, Wi-Fi country, locale and boot options.

command: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade
summary: Raspberry Pi's recommended update; full-upgrade also handles the dependency changes Pi OS ships more often than Debian.
example: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y

summary: Checks whether newer bootloader firmware is available on a Pi 4 or Pi 5; add -a to install it at the next reboot.
Shows which Raspberry Pi OS image you installed and its build date; cat /etc/os-release gives the Debian version.
Prints the exact board model and revision, e.g. Raspberry Pi 5 Model B Rev 1.0.
Shows whether you're running 64-bit (arm64) or 32-bit (armhf) Raspberry Pi OS, which decides what software you can install.
Lists connected camera modules and their sensor modes; plain rpicam-hello opens a live preview.
install: Built in (Bookworm and later; formerly libcamera-hello)

summary: Takes a full-resolution photo with the camera module; it replaced libcamera-still and raspistill.
Records 10 seconds of video; a Pi 5 writes MP4 directly, while older boards need --codec libav.
Shows a GPIO pin's mode and level; plain pinctrl lists every pin. It replaces the old raspi-gpio tool.
Sets GPIO17 as an output and drives it high (3.3 V), e.g. to light an LED; dl drives it low again.
Draws your board's GPIO header in the terminal with every pin number, power pin and ground pin labeled.
install: Built in on most images (else sudo apt install python3-gpiozero)

summary: Fetches only a page's headers (status code, server, redirects), a quick check of whether a site is up.
install: Built in (Windows 10/11 as curl.exe, macOS, most Linux)

summary: Downloads a file under its original name, following redirects; in Windows PowerShell type curl.exe.
install: Built in (Windows 10/11 as curl.exe, macOS, most Linux)

summary: Prints your public IP address, the one websites see.
install: Built in (Windows 10/11 as curl.exe, macOS, most Linux)

summary: Logs into another computer's terminal securely, such as a Raspberry Pi or home server.
Creates a modern SSH key pair for password-free, more secure logins.
Copies files to or from another machine over SSH.
Tunnels a remote port to your machine, so a device's web page opens at localhost:8080 in your browser.
Confirms Docker is installed and working by running a tiny test container.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Starts a container in the background and maps its port 80 to localhost:8080 on your machine.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Lists containers with their status, ports and names; drop -a to see only running ones.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Streams a container's log output live.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Opens a shell inside a running container so you can look around or fix things.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Starts every service in a compose.yaml in the background, the standard way to self-host apps.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Stops and removes a stack's containers and network; named volumes and their data are kept.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Downloads newer images for a stack; follow with docker compose up -d to switch over.
example: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Shows how much disk space images, containers, volumes and build cache are using.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Deletes dangling (untagged) images after asking for confirmation, reclaiming disk space.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh

summary: Opens a throwaway Ubuntu shell that disappears when you exit, perfect for testing commands safely.
install: Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS) · Linux/Pi: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh && sudo sh get-docker.sh
